title: Days, the poem
hookLine: in his poem Days, the days pass like silent gift-bearers and he takes only a few herbs

cards: A procession goes past a garden, single file, no end to it. The walkers are barefoot and silent, wrapped so you can't see their faces. Each one carries something: some carry crowns, some bundles of sticks for the fire.
Each stops in front of whoever is watching and offers a gift, whatever that person wants. A man sits in his garden and watches them go by. One stops in front of him.
That's the scene of a short poem Emerson called Days. The walkers are the days themselves, and what the man picks is the reason the poem stings.

teach.b: First, the disguise. The poem opens, "Daughters of Time, the hypocritic Days." Hypocritic is an odd word for a day.
Emerson means they wear a mask. A day looks plain, one more Tuesday, and hides what it's carrying.
Second, the offer: "To each they offer gifts after his will, Bread, kingdoms, stars, and sky that holds them all." Bread at one end, the whole sky at the other.
Each day, the poem says, offers whatever you're willing to ask for, from the smallest need to the largest wonder. Third, what he took. The man forgets what he wished for that morning.
He reaches out, and he "Took a few herbs and apples, and the Day Turned and departed silent." Not wrong, not wicked, just small: less than was offered, out of hurry or habit.
Then, too late, the poem says, he saw the Day's scorn under her solemn headband.

Earlier on this path, in an essay, Emerson pictured the days as veiled figures bearing gifts. In the poem, the blame turns on the watcher: he forgot his morning wishes. It isn't a poem about doing more.
Herbs and apples are good things. It's about noticing what's being held out, and asking for something real: a conversation instead of a scroll, an hour outside instead of one more errand.

how: Days is a short poem often read aloud or memorized by readers of Emerson, as a reminder to notice what each ordinary day offers.

games.q: you're the man in the garden. a silent Day stops in front of you, holding out bread, kingdoms, stars and sky. you've forgotten your morning wishes. what does the poem say you do?
o: take a few herbs and apples.
games.why: he hastily takes a few herbs and apples, and the Day turns and leaves. too late, he sees her scorn.

practice: Go back to the start of your own day, or the last quiet moment you had, and look for a wish in it: to call someone, to be outside for an hour, to make something, or to rest. Let one forgotten wish come back.
Then ask what today could hand you toward it, if you asked for more than herbs.
